output:
*Interview with Félix Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Monsieur Monnier, please. I am sorry to keep you up. I know you have had a terrible shock.

FÉLIX: Shock. Yes. I keep thinking I will wake up. I was in the library with my glass, and now there are policemen in the hall and I don't know what I am supposed to say. Forgive me, Monsieur l'Inspecteur. I talk when I am frightened. My mother always said so.

MATTHEY: You are doing well. Let us not start with the worst of it. Tell me about the dinner.

FÉLIX: It was the usual. When the temple bell struck nine, my watch showed twenty minutes to nine. My uncle made a scene about it in front of everyone. It was my father's watch, you understand. My father was Jules, Uncle Aurèle's younger brother. He died in 1889, and Dr Vauthier attended him in his last illness. The watch has run badly for ten years. I have never let anyone regulate it, not even my uncle, who has been offering for ten years.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

FÉLIX: I went up to the library and stayed there alone. I had brandy. I know, it was his brandy. The library is directly under the atelier, you know that. His pine floor is my ceiling. I sat with my glass and thought about money, which is what I always think about.

MATTHEY: Money?

FÉLIX: I owe some. Some of it to Bastien Girard. My uncle would have been very disappointed, but he was always disappointed in me. He knew everything about watches and nothing about his nephew.

MATTHEY: Tell me what you heard.

FÉLIX: At eighteen minutes past ten by my watch I heard a thump on the floor right above me, in the atelier. Then his repeater sounded. I know that sound better than my own name. Ten slow deep notes, I counted those. Then some doubled notes. Then quick high ones that I did not count, because I was listening to the floor.

MATTHEY: Take your time.

FÉLIX: At a quarter past ten by my watch, someone went quickly up the stairs past the library door. At twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, someone came quickly down. I did not see who. The door was shut, and I did not open it. I have thought about that again and again since, and I wish I had.

MATTHEY: Did you know what the sounds were?

FÉLIX: How could I? I thought it was him, working late, as he always does. I did not think anything. I drank.

MATTHEY: Who came to the library next?

FÉLIX: Bastien Girard came in at thirty-two minutes past ten by my watch. He wanted to talk about the repeater. He wanted to buy it, my uncle would not sell, and they quarrelled about the price at dinner. I think Girard also wanted to talk about my debts, but he did not say so. We sat together in the library until the temple struck eleven.

MATTHEY: You sat together until the temple struck eleven.

FÉLIX: Yes. Until the temple struck eleven.

MATTHEY: Monsieur Monnier, I must ask you to tell me only what you saw and heard. Nothing more.

FÉLIX: I understand. But you must understand what it looks like. The heir, alone in the library, directly under the bench where he was found. I know how it will sound when someone repeats it. I am not a brave man, Inspector. I only want to go to bed.

MATTHEY: Then tell me what you know, and we will be finished sooner.

FÉLIX: That is all I know. The thump. The repeater. The stairs, twice. Bastien, until eleven. My father's watch, which is wrong, and my uncle, who laughed at it.
